Research indicates that the most realistic/practical boundaries for most C/Z's and T/A's are those which would be defined by the population-mileage formula as proposed in the Commission's interim report served January 12, 1976, on Ex Parte No. MC-37 (Sub-No. 26), Commercial Zones and Terminal Areas.
Research results relevant to questions 4-11 form the basis for answers to questions 1-3. They are discussed below.
Provision of goods and services to consumer residents is a primary function essential to every municipality and settlement. In order to service populations as efficiently as possible, commercial activities are spatially distributed within cities in general agreement with population distribution. 1/
After the end of World War II, movements of people, commerce, and industry to locations farther and farther away from municipal centers accelerated. The suburban housing boom was underway almost as soon as the U.S. won the war. By 1950, the suburban population in urban fringes of urbanized areas was still only 13.9% of total U.S. population. By 1970, this suburban population had almost doubled as a percent and was 26.8% of the U.S. population. From 1950 to 1970, the fringe population grew by 161% while the population of central cities increased only 32% and declined from 32.3% to 31.4% as a percentage of total population. 2 /
Table 1 shows the extent to which the urban fringe populations of twenty cities grew from 1950-1960 and 1960-1970 relative to population changes in the central cities. With few exceptions, urban fringe populations expanded dramatically relative to much lower percentage gains (or losses) in central cities. 3/
The only case of an urban fringe population which failed to grow during a decade was Memphis in 1960-1970, and this one decrease was undoubtedly effected by annexation. Some of the urban fringe populations grew in spite of large losses to the central cities through annexation, Phoenix in 1950-1960 being the most notable case.
